title: A Daily Fiber Supplement Eased Knee Arthritis Pain
hook: In a six-week trial, a spoonful of chicory-root fiber cut knee osteoarthritis pain about as well as physiotherapy — and people actually stuck with it. Only 3.6% dropped out, versus 21%.
key_points: The INSPIRE trial randomized 117 adults with knee osteoarthritis to inulin, digital physiotherapy-supported exercise, both, or placebo, over six weeks.
Inulin is a prebiotic fiber from chicory root and Jerusalem artichoke, taken as a daily supplement.
Inulin and physiotherapy each reduced knee pain independently.
Only the inulin group also improved grip strength and lowered pain sensitivity.
Adherence differed sharply: 3.6% dropped out of the supplement group versus 21% of the physiotherapy group.
Proposed route: inulin feeds gut bacteria that make butyrate and raise GLP-1, a hormone tied to pain regulation and muscle health.
content_html: Knee osteoarthritis advice usually starts and ends with exercise, which works — if you keep doing it. A trial from the University of Nottingham tested something considerably easier to stick with: a daily scoop of fiber. Published in Nutrients, the INSPIRE trial randomized 117 adults with knee osteoarthritis into four groups over six weeks — inulin alone, digital physiotherapy-supported exercise alone, both together, or placebo.
extra_html:
Inulin is a prebiotic fiber found in chicory root and Jerusalem artichokes. In the trial, inulin and physiotherapy each reduced knee pain independently of one another. The more surprising results were the extras: only the inulin group showed improved grip strength and reduced pain sensitivity — measures you'd more readily associate with an exercise programme. And the two arms parted ways on something trials often bury: 3.6% of participants taking the supplement dropped out, compared with 21% of those in the physiotherapy group.

The mechanism the researchers propose runs through the gut. Inulin feeds beneficial bacteria, which produce short-chain fatty acids like butyrate and increase levels of GLP-1 — the same gut hormone behind drugs like Ozempic — which is associated with pain regulation and muscle health. Senior author Professor Ana Valdes called "the link we observed between GLP-1 and grip strength" particularly intriguing, while lead author Dr. Afroditi Kouraki framed the finding as raising "the exciting possibility that a simple dietary change" could meaningfully reduce pain. Worth keeping the scale in view: 117 people, six weeks, and a supplement rather than a drug. This is a promising lead, not a replacement for moving your knee.

related.title: Easing Knee Arthritis Without Surgery
related.hook: Knee osteoarthritis often ends in joint replacement. A minimally invasive procedure that blocks the inflammation-feeding blood vessels eased pain for at least a year — no surgery.

related.title: How Much Exercise You Actually Need
related.hook: The headline number is smaller than most people fear: about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week — roughly 20-some minutes a day — moves the needle on your health.

flashcards.prompt: What set the inulin group apart from the physiotherapy group in the INSPIRE trial?

choices.text: Only inulin also improved grip strength and lowered pain sensitivity
Only physiotherapy reduced knee pain at all
Inulin worked but caused more dropouts

flashcards.explanation_html: Both interventions reduced knee pain independently. But improved grip strength and lower pain sensitivity showed up only in the inulin group — and its dropout rate was 3.6% versus 21% for physiotherapy.

flashcards.prompt: What's the proposed gut–muscle–pain link behind inulin's effect?
flashcards.back_html: Inulin feeds beneficial gut bacteria, which produce short-chain fatty acids like butyrate and increase GLP-1 — a gut hormone associated with pain regulation and muscle health.

flashcards.prompt: Why does the dropout difference matter as much as the pain scores?
flashcards.back_html: Because a treatment only helps if people keep doing it. 3.6% quit the daily supplement versus 21% of the exercise programme — a simple dietary change may be easier to sustain than digital physiotherapy, even at similar effect on pain.
